The inverse design method prescribes desired distributions of angle of attack and axial induction factor along the blade.
The RANS/ADM computational model is used for the aerodynamic analysis, which models the effect of the turbine rotor as momentum sources without resolving the blade geometry.
The inverse design problem is solved using an iterative approach with the Trust-Region-Reflective optimization method.

The inverse design method is demonstrated for three test cases of conventional single-rotor wind turbines, including designing for the Betz optimum condition and reproducing the NREL 5 MW reference turbine blade geometry.
The inverse design methodology is extended to multi-rotor wind turbines, specifically the dual-rotor wind turbine configuration.
The mesh sensitivity study found that a grid resolution of 101x229 cells is sufficient for the RANS/ADM solver.
The Trust-Region-Reflective method is found to be more stable and better able to handle constraints on the blade design compared to the multi-dimensional Newton iteration method.
Prescribing angle of attack distributions in the inverse design avoids the multi-valued nature of the angle of attack-lift coefficient curve.
RANS CFD can simulate turbulent wake mixing effects, which potential flow methods cannot, allowing the inverse design to explore designs that maximize wake mixing and minimize wake losses.
The inverse design method is general enough to work for turbines with an arbitrary number of rotor disks, and is not limited to dual-rotor configurations.
The initial guess of the blade geometry has a significant impact on the convergence rate of the inverse design algorithm.
The inverse design algorithm is able to converge to the desired blade designs in all the test cases considered.
The final blade designs obtained using the inverse method have typical wind turbine blade characteristics, such as tapering chord and twist distributions.
The inverse design method can be used to explore blade designs that maximize annual energy production while satisfying manufacturing and transportation constraints.
The RANS/ADM computational model used in this study has been previously validated against experimental data for wind turbine aerodynamic performance prediction.
